units.title: Unit 49 — Ways of speaking
units.source: English Collocations in Use — Intermediate (2nd Edition); printed pages 102–103 (PDF pages 106–107).
units.bookTitle: English Collocations in Use — Intermediate (2nd Edition)
learningObjectives: Choose natural verb–noun and verb–adverb combinations for speeches, jokes, promises and requests.
Handle workplace conversations using tactful expressions for raising, changing and clarifying a subject.
Distinguish starting a conversation, joining one and making polite conversation.
Avoid learner errors with tell/say, speak/talk, give/make instructions and lengthy/large discussion.

items.example: The team leader will make a speech at the annual celebration.
items.note: Make a speech means deliver a prepared talk to an audience; do a speech is not the usual wording.

items.example: Could you get to the point so we can make a decision?
items.note: Used to ask someone to state the main idea without unnecessary details.

items.example: My grandfather loves to tell stories about life on the farm.
items.note: We tell stories rather than say stories; stories can be true, fictional or amusing.

items.example: Please do not give your word unless you intend to keep the promise.
items.note: To give your word is to make a serious personal promise, often to someone else.

items.pt: fazer uma piada; soltar uma piada
items.example: She tried to crack a joke to ease the tension before the interview.
items.note: Crack a joke is a common informal alternative to tell a joke, often suggesting a spontaneous remark.

items.example: He tried to tell a joke, but nobody understood the punchline.
items.note: Tell a joke is the usual pairing; say a joke is unnatural in this use.

items.example: I wish you luck with the final stage of your application.
items.note: A natural formula for expressing good wishes; the pronoun changes with the person addressed.

items.example: Can we have a brief chat about tomorrow’s timetable?
items.note: Brief chat suggests an informal, short conversation.

items.example: I need to have a quick word with the receptionist before we leave.
items.note: Often followed by with someone; a polite way to request a short private conversation.

items.example: Money can be a delicate subject between close friends.
items.note: Delicate suggests sensitivity and a need for tact, not physical fragility.

items.pt: uma discussão longa; uma conversa prolongada
items.example: The proposal led to a lengthy discussion about costs.
items.note: Lengthy describes something that takes a long time; large discussion is unnatural.

items.pt: levantar o assunto; trazer o tema à conversa
items.example: I did not want to raise the subject during lunch.
items.note: Raise introduces a topic for others to discuss; bring up the subject is another common option.

items.pt: falar em caráter não oficial; falar extraoficialmente
items.example: The official agreed to speak off the record about the negotiations.
items.note: Information shared off the record is not intended for public quotation or attribution; the understanding should be agreed in advance.

items.example: The supervisor will give instructions before the safety drill.
items.note: Use give instructions, not make instructions, when telling someone how to do a task.

items.pt: questionar alguém diretamente; confrontar alguém de forma direta
items.example: It may be better to challenge someone directly than to complain behind their back.
items.note: Challenge here means openly question a person or their actions; directly describes an explicit approach.

items.pt: alegar desconhecimento; dizer que não sabe
items.example: When asked about the missing files, the assistant pleaded ignorance.
items.note: A somewhat formal expression meaning claim not to know about something; it does not establish whether the claim is true.

items.pt: reclamar amargamente; queixar-se com muita indignação
items.example: Residents complained bitterly about the repeated water cuts.
items.note: Bitterly intensifies complain and suggests strong resentment or disappointment.

items.pt: dar uma indireta; deixar uma dica
items.example: She dropped a hint that she might move abroad next year.
items.note: To drop a hint is to suggest something indirectly instead of stating it outright.

items.example: His calm tone of voice helped everyone relax.
items.note: This noun phrase refers to how someone sounds and the attitude or emotion their voice conveys.

items.example: I would like to have a word with you after the meeting.
items.note: Often have a word with someone; it can signal a private or slightly serious conversation.

items.example: Please make it clear which documents we must submit.
items.note: Often followed by that or a question clause; it means state something without ambiguity.

items.example: When the questions became personal, he changed the subject.
items.note: The natural phrase is change the subject, not move the subject.

items.example: If you tell the truth now, it will be easier to resolve the problem.
items.note: Tell the truth contrasts with tell a lie; say the truth is generally not the standard expression.

items.example: Could I ask a favour before you head home?
items.note: Often ask someone a favour or ask a favour of someone; British spelling favour.

items.section: C · Advice column and social interaction
items.example: It is easier to get into conversation when everyone shares an interest.
items.note: Means start talking with someone socially, especially where conversation does not begin automatically.

items.pt: participar de uma conversa em andamento
items.section: C · Advice column and social interaction
items.example: I was too nervous to join in a conversation with the visiting researchers.
items.note: Join in means take part in an existing activity or exchange; compare strike up a conversation.

items.pt: puxar conversa por educação; manter conversa cordial
items.section: C · Advice column and social interaction
items.example: We made polite conversation while waiting for the guests to arrive.
items.note: Usually refers to light, socially appropriate small talk rather than a deep discussion.

items.section: C · Advice column and social interaction
items.example: The trainee made an interesting observation about customer behaviour.
items.note: An observation here is a comment or insight, not necessarily a scientific measurement.

items.section: C · Advice column and social interaction
items.example: You should address someone politely even when you disagree with them.
items.note: Address means speak to someone; politely describes the manner, not a postal address.

items.section: C · Advice column and social interaction
items.example: The manager apologised profusely for the booking mistake.
items.note: Profusely means very much or repeatedly; use British spelling apologise.

items.section: C · Advice column and social interaction
items.example: He struck up a conversation with another passenger at the bus stop.
items.note: Strike up means initiate a new conversation, often with a stranger; contrast join in an existing one.

items.pt: uma pausa na conversa; um momento de silêncio
items.section: C · Advice column and social interaction
items.example: During a lull in the conversation, I went to get some water.
items.note: A lull is a temporary period of quiet in an otherwise active exchange.

items.section: C · Advice column and social interaction
items.example: She whispered softly so she would not wake the baby.
items.note: Softly adds gentleness or low volume to whisper; it is intentionally emphatic despite partial overlap.

items.section: C · Advice column and social interaction
items.example: He admitted that he had told a lie about where he was.
items.note: The normal expression is tell a lie, not say a lie.

items.example: It is useful to speak a foreign language when working with international colleagues.
items.note: Use speak English, speak French, or speak a foreign language; talk French is a learner error.

units.title: Unit 50 — Ways of walking
units.source: English Collocations in Use — Intermediate (2nd Edition); printed pages 104–105 (PDF pages 108–109).
units.bookTitle: English Collocations in Use — Intermediate (2nd Edition)
learningObjectives: Describe walks and runs with natural verb patterns and precise movement adjectives or adverbs.
Distinguish pace, stroll, stride, wander and pick your way by manner and intention.
Recognise metaphorical walking expressions for achievements, setbacks, decisions and social background.
Use context to separate literal running and walking from figurative uses in work and everyday life.

items.example: The hotel is close enough for us to go on foot.
items.note: On foot is the fixed phrase, not on feet or by feet; often used instead of driving.

items.pt: dar uma caminhada; sair para caminhar
items.example: We like to go for a walk after our evening meal.
items.note: A common way to say take a walk for pleasure or exercise.

items.pt: dar um passeio a pé; caminhar sem pressa
items.example: After lunch, we took a stroll along the seafront.
items.note: Stroll is a slow, relaxed walk; go for a stroll is also common.

items.example: Shall we go for a stroll around the garden?
items.note: This is especially natural in conversation and stresses walking for pleasure.

items.example: My sister likes to go running before work.
items.note: Go running refers to the physical activity; make running is not natural in this sense.

items.pt: sair para correr; dar uma corrida
items.example: I usually go for a run on Saturday mornings.
items.note: A specific bout of running, usually for exercise.

items.example: A brisk walk in the morning helps me feel more alert.
items.note: Brisk suggests an energetic, fairly fast pace; brusque does not describe a walk in this sense.

items.pt: andar de um lado para o outro; andar de cá para lá
items.example: She paced up and down outside the examination room.
items.note: Pacing repeatedly back and forth often suggests worry or impatience.

items.example: He took long steps to keep up with the taller hikers.
items.note: Take steps describes how a person moves physically; the same noun can be figurative in other contexts.

items.pt: uma caminhada fácil; um trajeto simples a pé
items.section: B · Adjectives and adverbs associated with walking
items.example: It is an easy walk from the station to the museum.
items.note: Easy refers to little difficulty or effort and does not necessarily mean slow.

items.section: B · Adjectives and adverbs associated with walking
items.example: The doctor suggested a gentle walk after lunch.
items.note: Gentle emphasises slow, unhurried effort, unlike easy, which describes difficulty.

items.section: B · Adjectives and adverbs associated with walking
items.example: I recognised his heavy steps on the wooden stairs.
items.note: Heavy can suggest weight, fatigue or mood as well as the force of each footfall.

items.section: B · Adjectives and adverbs associated with walking
items.example: With light steps, the dancer crossed the stage.
items.note: Light steps are soft or quiet and contrast with heavy steps.

items.pt: um passeio a pé sem pressa
items.section: B · Adjectives and adverbs associated with walking
items.example: We enjoyed a leisurely stroll through the old quarter.
items.note: Leisurely implies unhurried and relaxed movement, not a fast walk.

items.section: B · Adjectives and adverbs associated with walking
items.example: A gentle stroll beside the river was enough for the afternoon.
items.note: Gentle highlights a comfortable, slow pace.

items.pt: caminhar rapidamente; andar em ritmo acelerado
items.section: B · Adjectives and adverbs associated with walking
items.example: The nurse walked briskly towards the ward.
items.note: Briskly refers to purposeful energetic speed, often faster than an ordinary walk.

items.section: B · Adjectives and adverbs associated with walking
items.example: She walked swiftly through the corridor to catch the lift.
items.note: Swiftly is a slightly more formal alternative to quickly when describing movement.

items.pt: avançar com cuidado; escolher onde pisar
items.section: B · Adjectives and adverbs associated with walking
items.example: You must pick your way cautiously across the loose stones.
items.note: Pick your way means carefully choose each step over difficult or risky ground.

items.pt: perambular sem rumo; andar a esmo
items.section: B · Adjectives and adverbs associated with walking
items.example: After losing the map, we wandered aimlessly around the streets.
items.note: Both wander and aimlessly emphasise a lack of fixed direction or purpose.

items.pt: caminhar a passos largos com raiva
items.section: B · Adjectives and adverbs associated with walking
items.example: The customer strode angrily towards the counter.
items.note: Stride implies long, confident or forceful steps; angrily specifies the emotion.

items.pt: caminhar a passos largos com confiança
items.section: B · Adjectives and adverbs associated with walking
items.example: She strode confidently onto the stage.
items.note: Suggests purposeful, self-assured movement with long steps.

items.pt: caminhar a passos largos com determinação
items.section: B · Adjectives and adverbs associated with walking
items.example: The engineer strode purposefully towards the control room.
items.note: Purposefully adds the idea of a clear intention to the movement.

items.section: B · Adjectives and adverbs associated with walking
items.example: The actor took confident strides towards the audience.
items.note: A related noun-based form of stride confidently; it emphasises the steps themselves.

items.pt: dar passos decididos; avançar com determinação
items.section: B · Adjectives and adverbs associated with walking
items.example: She took purposeful strides towards the meeting room.
items.note: Purposeful describes deliberate, determined steps, often suggesting urgency.

items.section: B · Adjectives and adverbs associated with walking
items.example: He took angry strides across the room after the argument.
items.note: Describes long, forceful steps that express anger.

items.pt: passar numa prova com muita facilidade
items.section: C · Walking through life: figurative language
items.example: He was so well prepared that he walked the final exam.
items.note: An informal British use of walk meaning pass a test or examination very easily; less suitable in formal academic writing.

items.section: C · Walking through life: figurative language
items.example: My uncle is a walking encyclopaedia of local history.
items.note: A figurative compliment for someone with extensive factual knowledge; British spelling encyclopaedia.

items.section: C · Walking through life: figurative language
items.example: We ran into problems when the supplier changed the delivery date.
items.note: Run into means encounter unexpectedly; problems need not involve physical movement.

items.word: people from all walks of life
items.pt: pessoas de todas as camadas sociais; pessoas de diferentes origens
items.section: C · Walking through life: figurative language
items.example: The festival attracted people from all walks of life.
items.note: Walks of life refers to different social backgrounds, occupations and experiences.

items.pt: tomar uma decisão precipitadamente; decidir sem refletir
items.section: C · Walking through life: figurative language
items.example: We should not rush headlong into a decision without checking the risks.
items.note: Headlong intensifies rush and suggests acting too quickly without sufficient thought.

items.section: C · Walking through life: figurative language
items.example: The new company took its first faltering steps during a difficult year.
items.note: A figurative expression for beginning something with uncertainty or limited experience.

items.pt: dar passos cautelosos; começar de modo hesitante
items.section: C · Walking through life: figurative language
items.example: The two organisations took tentative steps towards cooperation.
items.note: Tentative stresses caution and uncertainty, especially at an early stage.

items.pt: dar passos cuidadosos; tomar medidas cautelosas
items.section: C · Walking through life: figurative language
items.example: The team took careful steps to improve the process without interrupting production.
items.note: Steps can mean actions or measures, rather than literal movements of the feet.

items.section: C · Walking through life: figurative language
items.example: The students have made great strides in their spoken English.
items.note: A figurative way to say achieve substantial progress, often followed by in or towards.

items.section: C · Walking through life: figurative language
items.example: The committee ran up against opposition from local residents.
items.note: Run up against means encounter resistance or a difficult obstacle, not literally run.

items.word: get off on the wrong foot
items.pt: começar com o pé esquerdo; começar mal uma relação
items.section: C · Walking through life: figurative language
items.example: We got off on the wrong foot, but our working relationship improved.
items.note: An idiom for beginning an interaction or relationship badly; contrast get off to a good start.

items.example: The patient was able to take a few steps without help.
items.note: Use take steps for individual physical steps; this can also be figurative with a different meaning.

items.example: On our day off we went for a long walk in the hills.
items.note: This exercise-supported pattern combines go for a walk with long to describe distance or duration.

items.example: When the rain began, the children broke into a run.
items.note: Break into a run means suddenly switch from walking or standing to running.

items.pt: sair correndo para escapar; tentar fugir rapidamente
items.example: When the alarm went off, the thief made a run for it.
items.note: A natural idiomatic version of make a run for, meaning attempt to escape quickly.

items.pt: correr sem olhar por onde vai; correr às cegas
items.example: The frightened boy ran blindly through the dark garden.
items.note: Literally, run without paying attention to obstacles or direction; figurative uses are possible.

items.pt: administrar uma empresa; gerir um negócio
items.example: She has managed to run a business while studying part-time.
items.note: Run can mean manage or operate an organisation rather than move quickly.

items.example: The conference ran smoothly despite the late changes.
items.note: Run smoothly means function or proceed without unexpected difficulties.

items.example: Buses run regularly between the airport and the city centre.
items.note: Run describes a public transport service operating on a timetable; regularly expresses frequency.
